lines.text: A king brought down, a republic born in blood, and a general who crowned himself emperor. This is the French Revolution and the age of Napoleon.
It begins with ideas. The Enlightenment taught Europe to trust reason and to ask what right kings and churches had to rule.
Jean-Paul Marat would become the revolution's fiercest journalist, calling for the death of its enemies.
Far to the east, Mikhail Kutuzov was a Russian soldier who would one day lead his country against Napoleon's invasion.
The Abbe Sieyes, a priest, would write the pamphlet that asked what the common people were, and answered that they were everything.
Jacques-Louis David would paint the revolution and then the emperor, from the death of Marat to Napoleon crossing the Alps.
Louis the Sixteenth came to the throne in 1774, a king who would watch his power drain away and end on the scaffold.
His queen, Marie Antoinette, born in Austria, was blamed for lavish spending as France slid into debt.
Lafayette, a young nobleman, fought for American independence, and came home to lead the National Guard in the revolution's first years.
Maximilien Robespierre, a lawyer from Arras, would rise to lead the Jacobins and the Terror, until it consumed him too.
Across the Channel, Horatio Nelson would become Britain's greatest admiral and Napoleon's most dangerous foe at sea.
Georges Danton, a thundering orator, would help bring down the king, and later fall to the guillotine himself.
Josephine, born in Martinique, would marry Napoleon and become empress of the French.
Arthur Wellesley, later Duke of Wellington, would fight Napoleon's armies in Spain and finally beat him at Waterloo.
And in 1769, on Corsica, Napoleon Bonaparte was born, the soldier who would take hold of France and remake Europe.
Klemens von Metternich, an Austrian, would lead the peace that tried to put the old order back together.
In May 1789, with France out of money, Louis called the Estates-General of clergy, nobles and commoners, and lost control of it.
That year the Jacobin Club began meeting in a Paris convent. It would become the engine of the radical revolution.
Locked out of their hall in June, the commoners' deputies swore on a tennis court not to part until France had a constitution.
The revolution had begun, a decade of upheaval that would sweep away the absolute monarchy and the privileges of the nobles.
On the fourteenth of July a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, the fortress that stood for royal power. France still marks the day.
That summer came the Declaration of the Rights of Man: people are born free and equal in rights, and power comes from the nation.
In October thousands of women, angry at the price of bread, marched to Versailles and brought the king back to Paris.
In 1791 the royal family fled in disguise and were caught at Varennes. After that, few trusted the king.
That year, in the colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose up. Their revolution would end slavery there and create Haiti.
In 1792 France went to war with the crowned heads of Europe, wars that would spread its ideas by force and make Napoleon's name.
Volunteers from Marseille marched on Paris singing a new war song, the Marseillaise, now the national anthem.
The guillotine was adopted that year, meant as a quick and equal death. It would become the symbol of the Terror.
In August armed crowds stormed the Tuileries palace, and the monarchy was finished.
In September France was declared a republic.
In January 1793 Louis was tried by the Convention and beheaded in Paris.
In the west, the Vendee rose for church and king, and the republic crushed it with massacres.
Then the Terror. Mass arrests and the guillotine took thousands, the queen among them, as the revolution turned on its enemies, real and imagined.
In July 1794 Robespierre himself was arrested and executed, and the Terror came to an end.
A government of five directors took over, weak and divided, while a young general's fame grew.
In 1798 Napoleon invaded Egypt. The war failed, but the scholars he brought opened up the study of ancient Egypt.
At Aboukir Bay Nelson destroyed the French fleet, leaving Napoleon's army stranded.
Napoleon slipped home, and in November 1799 he and his allies overthrew the Directory. As First Consul, he now ruled France.
From 1803 France and its rivals fought again, more than a decade of war that would redraw the map of Europe.
Needing money, Napoleon sold Louisiana to the United States, roughly doubling the size of the young country.
In 1804 came his Civil Code, one clear law for property, contracts and family, which still shapes the law of many countries.
That same year the republic became an empire, with Napoleon at its head.
In December, in Notre-Dame, he placed the crown on his own head while the pope looked on.
In 1805 Nelson destroyed the French and Spanish fleets off Trafalgar. He died in the battle, but Britain ruled the seas.
On land, weeks later, Napoleon crushed Russia and Austria at Austerlitz, his greatest victory.
Unable to invade Britain, he banned all trade with it, a blockade that hurt Europe and pulled him into more wars.
In 1807 at Tilsit he and the Russian tsar divided Europe between them. It was the height of his power.
From 1808 Spain and Portugal fought back, with guerrillas and British help under Wellington, and the war slowly bled the French.
In 1812 Napoleon marched a huge army into Russia. Hunger, disease and winter destroyed it, and the tide of the wars turned.
Outside Moscow, Borodino was the bloodiest single day of these wars, and it opened the road to an empty, burning city.
In 1813 at Leipzig, the Battle of the Nations, Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden together beat him.
Napoleon abdicated and was sent to Elba, while in Vienna the powers met to redraw the map and restore the balance.
But in 1815 he escaped and ruled France once more, for about a hundred days.
At Waterloo, Wellington and the Prussians under Blucher defeated him for the last time. He was exiled to Saint Helena.
The Bourbon kings came back to the throne of France, yet the old world they had known was gone.
The kings returned, but the ideas of 1789 and Napoleon's code outlived them all.
